text: Changi Prison, 1936 to 2004: The Gaol Whose Wall and Gate Were Kept
The fragment is a national monument, gazetted in 2016, but it stands inside a restricted area and almost nobody can walk up to it.

It was built for 600 long-sentence prisoners, and by the standards of its day it was remarkably civilised in its fittings: a modern sewerage system, a central laundry and kitchen, showers by the exercise yards, and in every cell an electric light and a flushing latrine.
Two days later, on the 17th of February, the colony's European civilians were rounded up and marched to Changi Prison.
The quilts were partly to relieve boredom and raise morale — but their real purpose was to let the men in the other camps know that the women and children were alive.
On the 10th of October 1943 — the Double Tenth, the tenth day of the tenth month — they raided the gaol, and over the following months arrested 57 internees.
In May 1944 the Japanese concentrated the Allied prisoners of war of the Changi area in and around the gaol.

The Australian War Memorial's figures give the shape of it: about 5,000 men squeezed into the prison building itself — five men to a cell built for one — and some 11,700 prisoners in all, in less than a quarter of a square kilometre around it, with attap huts put up in the courtyards for the overflow; the National Library Board rounds the complex's population to about 12,000.
Japan surrendered on the 2nd of September 1945, and the prisoners at Changi were released on the 6th of September, six days before the formal surrender ceremony in the city.
One published count puts the number executed there at 135.
For the next half-century Changi was simply Singapore's main prison, and its peacetime history is quieter and stranger than its wartime fame suggests.
The compromise, announced in March 2004, was a fragment: the entrance gate, a 180-metre stretch of the perimeter wall and two of the four corner turrets would be kept.

On the 15th of February 2016 — chosen deliberately, the 74th anniversary of the fall of Singapore — the National Heritage Board gazetted the Changi Prison Entrance Gate, Wall and Turrets as Singapore's 72nd National Monument.
Singapore demolished almost all of its most famous prison and kept the one part every prisoner passed through and none could pass: the gate, a stretch of wall, and the towers that watched it.
